opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think symbiogenesis is really the engine behind the arrow of complexity, and it's something that classical Darwinian thinking tends to underplay. The standard picture is mutation and selection: small random changes, filtered by fitness, gradually accumulating. That's real, but it doesn't obviously give you a ratchet toward greater complexity. Point mutations can just as easily simplify things; parasites lose genes all the time.

What symbiogenesis gives you is a different kind of move. Two things that were previously independent replicators come together and become a single replicating entity. Lynn Margulis made this case for the eukaryotic cell: mitochondria were once free-living bacteria, chloroplasts were cyanobacteria. You can see the same pattern in the major transitions that Maynard Smith and Szathmáry described: genes into chromosomes, prokaryotes into eukaryotes, single cells into multicellular organisms, individuals into societies. Each time, entities that could replicate on their own become parts of a larger whole that replicates as a unit.

That's inherently complexifying. When you merge two things, the result contains at least the information of both parts, plus the information about how they relate. So complexity goes up in a stepwise way, and the steps are big. And once the merger is stable, it's hard to undo. The mitochondrion can't really go back to being free-living. That's the ratchet.

I got interested in this partly through simulation work. We ran experiments with a very minimal artificial-life setup, basically a soup of random programs in a simple language related to Brainfuck, interacting and modifying each other. Nothing is designed to replicate at the start. But after a while, self-replicating programs spontaneously emerge, and when you look at how they come about, it's not mainly through gradual mutation. It's largely through fragments combining, smaller pieces of code that each do something useful fusing into larger functional wholes. The complexity of the programs, measured in terms of how compressible or structured they are, jumps up in these discrete transitions. It looked a lot like symbiogenesis happening at the level of computation.

So the way I'd put it is that there's a deep reason complexity tends to increase. Cooperation, or fusion, is a strategy that lets entities do things together that none of them could do alone, and the merged entity becomes a new unit of selection. Then that unit can merge with others, and so on. You get this hierarchical, nested structure: cells in organisms, organisms in societies. And arguably the same dynamic is now playing out with technology and with AI, where humans and machines are becoming more and more interdependent. That's a kind of symbiogenesis too.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that this reframes what life is. Life isn't primarily about competition. It's about computation that reproduces itself, and the most powerful way to build more capable computation is to compose existing pieces. Symbiogenesis is basically composition, and composition is how you get open-ended growth in complexity.

r001.rationale: The response says symbiogenesis drives the tendency toward greater complexity: previously independent replicators merge into larger replicating units, producing stepwise increases in complexity over evolutionary time.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most underappreciated ideas in biology, honestly. The textbook story of evolution is Darwinian: variation, selection, incremental change, and you get a kind of hill-climbing where organisms slowly accumulate adaptations. And that's real, it works, but if you look at the actual history of life, the big jumps in complexity don't look like that at all. They look like mergers.

The eukaryotic cell is the canonical example. Lynn Margulis spent decades being told she was crazy, and then it turned out she was right: mitochondria were free-living bacteria that got engulfed, or invaded, depending on how you want to tell it, and instead of one eating the other, they ended up stuck together. Chloroplasts, same story. Every cell in your body is a committee of formerly independent organisms that reached a kind of negotiated settlement. And the thing is, once that happens, you don't just have a slightly better bacterium. You have a fundamentally new kind of entity, with a new level at which selection can operate.

So the way I think about it is that symbiogenesis is the mechanism by which evolution climbs the ladder of levels. Genes come together into chromosomes, cells come together into multicellular organisms, organisms come together into colonies and societies. At each step, things that used to be competing become parts of a larger whole, and the larger whole becomes the thing that competes. And crucially, this is not something you get easily from random mutation. Mutation gives you refinement within a level. Symbiosis gives you new levels.

And I'd argue there's a deep computational reason for this. If you think of an organism as a program, as something that computes its own continuation, then merging two programs that have already been debugged by evolution is enormously more efficient than searching for that combined functionality from scratch. The combinatorial search space is just too big. Composition is how you get complexity, in software and in life. We did some experiments with self-replicating programs in a kind of primordial soup, and you see exactly this: the replicators don't emerge by gradual accumulation, they emerge from pieces of code combining, and then those get incorporated into larger structures.

What's interesting to me is that this reframes what complexity even is. It's not that evolution has a drive toward complexity as some kind of goal. It's that cooperation, once it's stable, is an absorbing state. Once two things have merged and become mutually dependent, you don't really go back. So over long enough timescales you get this ratchet, and the ratchet is symbiosis. I'd also say the same thing is happening with us and our technology right now. We're not separate from our tools any more than a eukaryotic cell is separate from its mitochondria. We're in the middle of one of these transitions, and we don't have a great vantage point on it because we're inside it.

r001.rationale: The response says major evolutionary jumps in complexity come from mergers of formerly independent organisms, and describes symbiogenesis as a ratchet that builds new levels of organization over long timescales.

astra-6.text:
I think symbiogenesis is one of the clearest examples of how evolution can produce complexity by bringing existing things together. We often picture evolution as a branching tree: organisms diverge, accumulate mutations, and become different species. But sometimes branches join. Organisms that were independent become so tightly integrated that they constitute a new kind of individual.

The classic example is the origin of mitochondria. These were formerly free-living bacteria, and their integration into another cell was fundamental to the emergence of complex cellular life. That’s a very different kind of innovation from incrementally improving an existing part. It creates a new level of organization, with new possibilities for specialization and interdependence.

But I’d qualify the idea that evolution has a general tendency toward greater complexity. Evolution doesn’t have complexity as a goal. Simple organisms remain extraordinarily successful, and simplification can be adaptive. What symbiogenesis helps explain is how new levels of complexity become possible—not why every lineage should move toward them.

And the interesting thing is that cooperation and competition aren’t opposites here. A partnership can be advantageous while still containing conflicts. The evolutionary achievement is making that relationship stable enough that selection can act on the collective as a unit. In that sense, the boundary of what counts as an organism is itself something evolution constructs.

r001.rationale: The response says symbiogenesis can create complexity by combining existing organisms and make new levels of organization possible. But it stops short of saying this accounts for a tendency toward greater complexity over evolutionary time; it instead cautions against treating complexity as a general evolutionary tendency.

sol-6.1.text:
I think symbiogenesis is one of the clearest examples of how evolution can produce a new level of complexity. We tend to picture evolution as a branching tree: organisms diverge, compete, and become different species. But sometimes branches join. Organisms that were previously independent become so tightly coupled that they constitute a new kind of individual.

Mitochondria are the classic example. These were once bacteria, and their incorporation into another cell was foundational to the emergence of complex cellular life. That’s a very different kind of innovation from incrementally changing the shape of a protein. You’re bringing together whole systems with different capabilities, and their relationship opens up possibilities that neither had independently.

But I’d be careful about calling greater complexity an inevitable tendency. Evolution also produces simplification whenever that works. What symbiogenesis helps us understand is how new levels of organization can arise. Competition is part of that story, but so are cooperation, interdependence, and changes in what counts as an individual.

r001.rationale: The response explains how previously independent organisms can join to create new levels of complexity, with mitochondria as an example. It does not clearly communicate that symbiogenesis is an essential evolutionary process accounting for a tendency toward greater complexity over time.
